unesco.title: Mak Yong theatre
unesco.description:
This ancient theatre form created by Malaysia’s Malay communities combines acting, vocal and instrumental music, gestures and elaborate costumes. Specific to the villages of Kelantan in northwest Malaysia, where the tradition originated, Mak Yong is performed mainly as entertainment or for ritual purposes related to healing practices. 

Experts believe that Mak Yong appeared well before the Islamization of the country. It was performed as a royal theatre under the direct patronage of the Kelantan Sultanate until the 1920s. Hence, the tradition was perpetuated in a rural context without forsaking the numerous refinements acquired at court, such as sophisticated costume design. A typical Mak Yong performance opens with an offering followed by dances, acting and music as well as improvised monologues and dialogues. A single story can be presented over several consecutive nights in a series of three-hour performances. In the traditional village setting, the performances are held on a temporary open stage built of wood and palm leaves. The audience sits on three sides of the stage, the fourth side being reserved for the orchestra consisting of a three-stringed spiked fiddle (rebab), a pair of doubleheaded barrel drums (gendang) and hanging knobbed gongs (tetawak). Most roles are performed by women, and the stories are based on ancient Malay folk tales peopled with royal characters, divinities and clowns. Mak Yong is also associated with rituals in which shamans attempt to heal through song, trance-dance and spirit possession. 

Mak Yong, which requires long years of training, has been preserved until the present largely through oral transmission. In today’s society, few young people are willing to commit to such rigorous apprenticeships. As a result, this important tradition is undergoing steady decline, as attested by reduced dramatic and musical repertories and a shortage of seasoned performers.

profile.name: Mak Yong
profile.tagline: Malaysia's ancient all-female theatre-dance combining court refinement and ritual.
profile.insight: UNESCO inscribed Mak Yong as intangible heritage, preserving a pre-Islamic Kelantanese court tradition featuring all-female casts, rebab music, and ancient animist rituals.
profile.profile: Mak Yong is a traditional form of dance theatre practiced among the Malays in Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Originating in pre-Islamic times, it combines acting, vocal and instrumental music, elaborate costumes, and improvised dialogues. Most roles are traditionally performed by women, alongside male clowns. Though banned in Kelantan for its animist elements, it survived through diaspora and village traditions.
profile.profile_long: Mak yong is a traditional form of dance theatre practiced among the Malays particularly in Kelantan, Terengganu, Yala, Pattani, Riau, and North Sumatra. Although most traditional Malay dances were influenced by India, Java, and other parts of Southeast Asia, mak yong's singing and musical repertoire are unique to the region. Of the major stories performed in mak yong, most are derived from Kelantan or Patani mythology, such as 'Anak Raja Gondang'. Historically, a traditional performance begins by placing an offering (semah kampung) to placate and pay respect to spirits or previous performers. This is followed by dancing, acting, and improvised dialogues presented over several nights. The lead dancer is called the Pak Yong and dresses like a king, accompanied by a queen, palace girls, and male jesters. A group called Jong Dongdang sings and dances in between chapters and at the story's closing. The mak yong orchestra features the rebab, a three-stringed spiked lute, double-headed barrel drums (gendang), and a pair of gongs, alongside the flute (serunai), keduk drums, and small cymbals (kesi). Mak yong was originally a form of folk theatre involving rituals connected with propitiation and healing, such as the main puteri trance-dance. Believed to be at least 800 years old and rooted in pre-Islamic native animism, it later received patronage from the Kelantan Sultanate. In 1991, the Islamic party government in Kelantan banned mak yong for its un-Islamic elements and clothing, but the ban was lifted in 2019. UNESCO declared mak yong theatre a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, though it faces a decline today due to a shortage of young apprentices willing to undergo rigorous training.

sections.origins_and_history: Mak yong originated in the Pattani Kingdom and spread to Kelantan and Kedah over 200 years ago. Passed down orally among villagers, it is estimated to be at least 800 years old. It was patronized by the Kelantan Sultanate until the 1920s. In 1991, Kelantan banned mak yong for its animist elements and women's clothing, but the ban was lifted in 2019.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances open with an offering (semah kampung) followed by dancing, acting, and improvised dialogues across three-hour shows over several nights. Most roles are performed by women, featuring the Pak Yong (king), a queen, palace girls, and male jesters. A group called Jong Dongdang performs songs and dances between chapters.
sections.music_and_instruments: The orchestra features the rebab (a three-stringed spiked lute), gendang (double-headed barrel drums), a pair of gongs (tetawak), serunai (flute), keduk drums, and kesi (small cymbals). Its singing and musical repertoire are distinct and unique to the region.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances traditionally use elaborate costumes where the lead Pak Yong dresses like a king. In villages, performances are held on temporary open stages built of wood and palm leaves, with the audience sitting on three sides and the orchestra on the fourth.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Mak yong served as entertainment, harvest thanksgiving, and healing rituals (such as mak yong mak puteri involving trance-dancing and spirit possession). It acts as a mystical conduit to the spirit world and honors teachers and graduates.
sections.notable_figures: The late Cik Ning was a leading mak yong performer in the 1980s. Long Abdul Ghaffar supported the art in 1923 by building Kampung Temenggung on palace grounds, an effort later continued by Khatijah Awang's Seri Temenggong group.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include Makyong United (Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat), Makyong Kelantan, Makyong Kedah, Makyong Mar (Perlis and Satun), Makyong Riau (Indonesia), Field Makyong (Medan, Indonesia), and Makyong Kalimantan (Indonesia).
sections.lineage: Stories are derived from Kelantan or Patani mythology, including tales like 'Anak Raja Gondang' originating from Buddhist Jataka tales.

profile.sacred_note: Mak yong contains deep animist and pre-Islamic spiritual elements, historically involving offerings to spirits (semah kampung), spirit possession, and healing rituals (main puteri), which led to past religious bans.

teaching.formation: Audience sits on three sides of the stage, the fourth side being reserved for the orchestra.

music_profile.sound_description: Led by the three-stringed spiked lute (rebab), accompanied by double-headed barrel drums (gendang) and hanging knobbed gongs, creating a distinct traditional Malay theatrical sound.
